$comment: DRAFT. The OT system overlay, proposed in the operational technology domain document, 8.3, where its rules are S1 to S5. One overlay for every OT sector; the reference substation is its first worked example. S1, S2 and S4 are not specific to OT and now sit in the generic overlay system-disclosure, published in Release 1, which this profile extends. Each rule here names the S-rule it implements.
title: OT System Overlay (draft)

objective.$comment: C1. The consumer is the asset owner, or an assessor acting for one, receiving a system from an integrator. The generic overlay answers what the design uses and who provides its keys; this profile adds where each interface sits and which conduit it crosses.
objective.consumer: An asset owner, or an assessor acting for one, accepting an OT system from its integrator.
objective.decision: For each interface the design uses: which zone it sits in and which conduit it crosses, so that a migration of one component can be planned with the zones and conduits it affects.
decisionOptions: accept it and record the migration dependencies in the register
require the integrator to change the design before acceptance

scope.$comment: As the generic overlay: one system design, as its integrator delivers it.

productRules.note: The zones of the design, in the sense of IEC 62443-3-2. Each interface names one of them (I1).

productRules.description: S5. System states the IEC 62443-3-3 capability security level its integrator claims for it as delivered
productRules.note: S5. A claim the record reports, not a judgement it makes: the capability security level (SL-C) the integrator states for the system as delivered. SHOULD, because many systems in service were never assessed against IEC 62443-3-3, and a MUST would exclude them.

interfaceRules.note: S3. The zone the interface sits in, one of the zones the system names (P1).
S3. Whether the connection on this interface stays in its zone or crosses into another.

S3. The conduit the path crosses, as the bom-ref of the system component that implements it: a firewall, a VPN router or a gateway. A conduit is an interface of that device, not an object of its own. Withholdable, because a public record may not show the network design.

exclusions.item: Latency budgets, compensating controls and site variations
exclusions.reason: They belong in the asset owner's register, which describes sites, not the design.

exclusions.item: A timing class for each interface
exclusions.reason: An integration constraint of the product.

changelog.summary: First draft, built on the reference substation.
Extends the generic overlay system-disclosure. S1, S2 and S4 moved there.
